paras: The threatened lynching of Rafe Bird took place on the night of March 27, 1888, near Pooler, Georgia, when armed Pooler men took Bird, a Black farmer suspected in the killing of Joseph Gill, into a swamp and threatened to lynch him. Bird denied any part in the killing, named another Black man to save his life, and took the accusation back at daylight; he was jailed in Savannah and released in July when a grand jury declined to indict him. The Savannah Morning News followed the case into October, headlining Bird's "Narrow Escape from Lynching."

On the evening of March 23, Joseph Gill, about 27, was shot dead near Butler's avenue, about half a mile from Pooler, while lying in wait beside a slaughtered beef belonging to the Widow Farrell. According to the first report, he rose and called "drop that beef" to three Black men who came for the sacks, and one of them fired a shotgun into his breast. That night over twenty men searched the woods, and the paper predicted that if the "indignant citizens" found the killers, the county would hardly be put to the expense of trying them.

Coroner Dixon's jury returned a verdict of murder by "some party or parties unknown," and Gill's brothers testified that they could not say whether the thieves were white or Black. Bird, who rented land near the spot, told the inquest he had met two men on the railroad that afternoon, one carrying a musket like the one later found near the beef. Detective Wetherhorn found his stories conflicting and sent the Pooler men home to "use their judgment" in learning whether Bird's family had eaten liver.

On Tuesday afternoon, March 27, after Bird's daughter let slip that the family had eaten liver, Marion Gill, Ben Rothwell, Joseph Ferrill and Jack Gill seized Bird at his cabin, found part of a beef liver in a wash boiler, and took him bound to the railroad station.

Later that night, the Morning News reported, "a larger body of men, armed," took Bird from his guards into the swamp and threatened to lynch him if he did not tell the truth. In his own statement, Bird said his captors first tied his thumbs together and threatened to hang him by them, then carried him about a mile into the swamp around midnight and "said they was going to lynch me." To save his life he named a man called Brown at the four-mile hill, whom the party arrested and took to the station, and at daylight he said he "had been compelled to lie on somebody to save my life." The paper credited Henry Haywood's "presence of mind and considerate judgment" with saving Bird, saying the "enraged posse" listened to him.

Bird was jailed in Savannah, and Wetherhorn ordered the release of old Willis Brown of the four-mile post. A second Brown, hunted by a Pooler posse, hid after hearing of Bird's ordeal, then came to town with the preacher Miller and was released.

In July the superior court grand jury declined to indict Bird or Abram Edy, arrested in June, and both were discharged. In October Bird identified Fred Roland, a prisoner held for an assault and robbery, as the man with the musket; Roland denied killing Gill. No report of a trial for Gill's killing, or of any action against the men who threatened Bird, appears in the coverage.

All known coverage came from the Savannah Morning News, which reported the case from the morning after the killing into October. Its March 29 headlines announced "A Pooler Posse's Midnight Ride to the Swamp with the Prisoner" and "His Narrow Escape from Lynching," over Bird's statement, printed at length. The same reports described Bird as "a type of the thriftless and slovenly negro" and gave space to the detective's view of his "bad" character.

The paper did not criticize the posse, explaining that after finding the liver its members felt sure they had the right man. Its July summary said only that "the enraged citizens" had taken Bird to the swamps and by threats led him to accuse Brown.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Rafe Bird
bases: An armed party of Pooler men seized Rafe Bird, a Black suspect in a killing, bound him, took him into a swamp at night and threatened to hang or lynch him to force a confession, but did not kill him (A3, A6, A8); Joseph Gill's own death was a shooting by unidentified beef thieves, not mob violence (A1, A2).

A party of armed men acting on the accusation that Bird was connected with Gill's killing threatened to lynch him, but he survived and was jailed (A3, A6, A11); no one was killed by a mob, and Gill was killed by a thief, not a group acting under a pretext of justice (A1, A2).
All reports come from one paper, the Savannah Morning News, though it gave the threat in its own narrative, in Bird's signed-off statement, and in later recaps (A3, A6, A8, A11).

framing.detail: The Morning News anticipated summary justice for Gill's killers without disapproval, headlined Bird's 'Narrow Escape from Lynching', printed his account of the threats in full, and explained rather than criticized the posse.
Its reporters described Bird and Mathis in demeaning racial terms ('a type of the thriftless and slovenly negro') and gave prominence to the detective's view of Bird's 'bad character'.
